title: The shape of an argument
grammar: Nominalisation and word formation for academic style

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Sound objective and authoritative. Learn nominalisation and word formation for real academic style.
scene.intro: Serious writing has a shape of its own. Watch how an academic writer turns actions into nouns — fail into failure, decide into decision — and suddenly the argument sounds measured, objective, authoritative. In this unit you learn nominalisation and word formation, the exact skill tested in Part 3 of the exam, and the secret behind a strong C1 essay. For the Inspiring Nordic project, this is how your ideas earn respect. Let's begin.

activities.title: Reading — the reading club on academic style

data.title: The shape of an argument
data.author: sofia
data.text:
Read any serious essay and you will notice something curious: the people disappear. Where an everyday speaker says “the government failed, so voters got angry”, an academic writer prefers “the government's failure provoked public anger”. The events are the same; the grammar is transformed.

This trick has a name — nominalisation, the art of turning verbs and adjectives into nouns. Decide becomes decision; analyse becomes analysis; clear becomes clarity. In our Grade 11 club we tried rewriting a heated opinion as a cool academic paragraph, and Mateo admitted that it suddenly sounded far more authoritative — even though the ideas had not changed at all.

Why does this matter? Because nominalisation lets a writer sound objective and impersonal. Instead of blaming a named person, the sentence presents a process. Nadia noticed the danger too: hidden behind an abstract noun, responsibility can quietly vanish. “A mistake was made” tells us nothing about who made it.

Word formation is therefore both a tool and a test. Part 3 of the Cambridge exam asks you to build the right member of a word family from a single root — strong, strength, strengthen, strongly — and one wrong ending costs the mark. Liam keeps a notebook of these families, adding a new one every day.

For the Inspiring Nordic project, our essays must sound measured and formal without becoming lifeless. The best academic writing is precise, not pompous. Master nominalisation, use it sparingly, and your argument will have shape, weight and the quiet confidence that persuades a demanding reader.

data.title: Nominalisation and word formation
data.intro: Formal and academic English prefers nouns to verbs. By turning actions and qualities into nouns, we make writing sound objective and compact. Word formation — knowing the noun, verb, adjective and adverb in a family — is the key skill.

examples.text: The government's failure to act angered voters.
The discovery of the vaccine changed medicine.
A careful analysis of the data followed.
The clarity of her argument impressed everyone.

rules: Turn a verb or adjective into a noun to sound formal and objective: decide → decision, strong → strength.
In Part 3, read the whole sentence: the gap may need a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, a negative prefix (un-, in-, dis-) or a plural.

data.text: Academic English relies heavily {1} nouns. Instead of saying that prices rose sharply, a writer refers {2} a sharp rise in prices. This makes the argument sound objective, {3} it removes the person from the sentence. The transformation of verbs {4} nouns is called nominalisation, {5} is a hallmark of formal style. It is precision {6} readers of academic prose expect above all.

data.voice_note: Voz: la profesora (Miss Vega), sobre word formation.
data.script: Good morning, Grade 11. Today we practise word formation — the skill tested in Part 3 of the exam. From one root, English builds a family: decide, decision, decisive, decisively. Learning these families will transform your writing and your reading. In academic style, we often turn verbs into nouns; this process is called nominalisation. It makes an argument sound objective. Sofía will present her word map first on Monday. For homework, build five word families from the reading. Remember: a strong essay is precise, formal and impersonal. Bring your best examples.

activities.title: Speaking — rephrase in academic style. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, take a strong personal opinion and rephrase it in cool academic style, using nominalisation. Model: “Rather than ‘people waste water’, we might write: ‘the wastage of water remains a serious concern’.” 1) Does formal language make an argument fairer or just colder? 2) When does ‘objective’ writing hide who is responsible? 3) Which sounds stronger to you — a verb or its noun? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write a short academic paragraph (10–12 sentences) on a topic from the Inspiring Nordic project, using at least four nominalisations (e.g. failure, decision, analysis, improvement) to sound formal and objective. Capital letters and full stops!
